  "text": "By morning Tobias had worn a pale place in the brim of his hat.

He sat in the church until the woman who cleaned it came with her bucket. She asked if someone had died. He moved his knees so she could pass.

At nine he took the road to Maren’s house.

There were gulls again. One stood on the last fence post, pulling something white apart. The tide was where the tide ought to be.

He counted the posts without meaning to. Eleven. All sound. At the porch he put his hand against the wood, then took it away.

The door was shut but not latched.

Inside, the lamp stood on the sill. He touched the chimney with two fingers. Cold. The room smelled of lamp oil and the wool of an old rug.

He called her name once, in the voice he used when bringing fish.

There was a cup beside the sink, washed and turned down. Her coat hung on its hook. He had never known which things she took when she went out.

He waited until the church clock struck the half hour. Then he closed the door, lifting it a little so the latch would catch.

At the gate he looked back.

From there the sill was too high for him to see the lamp. He could see only the upper panes and a strip of ceiling, with its familiar stain above the chimney.

He stood looking at that stain.

  "text": "For three days Tobias went there after hauling his boat above the tideline. He brought nothing the first day. On the second he brought bread, and on the third he took the bread away.

The door stayed where he had left it. Rain darkened a narrow strip of floor.

He found a stone beside the step and set it against the door. It was not large enough. He went down to the beach for another.

By the following week people had begun asking him about the house rather than Maren. Was the roof sound. Had anyone spoken to her sister. What ought to be done with the hens.

There were no hens. He told them this each time.

One evening he took a cloth and dried the floor. He wrung the cloth over the sink, then folded it along the marks already worn into it. The cup was still turned down. A small brown spider had fastened a thread from its handle to the tap.

He left that alone.

Outside, someone was calling a child in from the road. Tobias waited for the child to answer. After a while he heard running feet, a complaint, a door.

He moved the stone with his boot and drew Maren’s door almost shut. The gap was no wider than his hand.

At home he cooked two potatoes because one always rolled about in the pan. He ate them standing up.

Before bed he hung his coat where he could reach it without lighting the lamp.",

  "text": "The first frost came while the boats were still out. Tobias returned with a split thumbnail and three fish too small to sell. He wrapped them in paper before going up the path.

At Maren’s step he stopped. There was nowhere to leave fish that would not bring cats.

He carried them home again.

In November her sister sent a letter addressed to the house. The postman gave it to Tobias outside the shop, holding it by one corner because his gloves were wet. Tobias put it inside his coat. That evening he laid it on the table beside the cup.

He had meant to turn the cup over. Instead he checked beneath the sink for a bucket.

The roof had begun to leak above the stairs. Not much: a dark patch, then a drop that gathered slowly and fell before he was ready to hear it. He moved the bucket twice. On his next visit he brought a scrap of sacking to quiet the bottom.

There were things he could do before winter. He wrote them on the back of a receipt. Nails. Putty. Ask about ladder.

The tide was low when he finished. From the doorway he could see the boats resting crookedly on the mud, each tied to something hidden beneath it.

He folded the receipt and put it away.
